reviews.review:
Filiy Eclipse is truly delightful, the kind of game that makes you gratetful to have found it. As someone who scrolls Steam new releases daily, finding something truly special has become rarer and rarer. But it’s all worth it, because sometimes you find Filiy Eclipse. 

Filiy Eclipse is more than anything else bizarre. The floaty movement, strange and slightly unpleasant music, and bewildering world and scenario all combine to make something that is truly strange and captivating. What’s especially cool is the way the game’s setting immediately confronts you. If you look up at the store screenshots you may notice very strange things going on with the horizon in the background. This is on purpose and it is wonderful, with it being just about the first thing you notice upon starting a new game. It’s a delightful bit of strangeness that gets your mind churning, forcing you to confront the game’s setting head on. You can probably figure out what exactly is going on pretty quick, but rest assured, the horizon is probably the least strange thing going on with with game’s world. 

The game's combat is something truly special as well. It’s definitely a hard sell since the game’s movement is so floaty and inaccurate. But the floatiness also means that everything has commitment, and luckily the game provides no shortage of strategic tools to use in combat. Something that isn’t clear at first is how heavily the game lets you build your own moveset. As you play you unlock skills that can map to one of six command inputs, most with fighting game quarter and half circle motions involved. What’s interesting is rather than letting you put any skill on any input like you see in other games that have similar systems; Filiy Eclipse instead restricts specific types of skills to specific inputs. So quarter circle forwards will always be a hadouken like thing and DP input will always be some sort of anti-air. One advantage of locking skills to specific inputs is the preservation of muscle memory allowing you to better master the combat system even while changing around the nuances of your build. In other games with similar systems, such as the modern Ys games, I never really developed any true knowledge of what buttons were good since what each button did changed so wildly over the course of the game. Instead in Ys especially I would get in the enemy's face and just spam buttons. It’s not too much of a problem in Ys, whose combat has always had a particular flavour of meatheadedness; but Filiy Eclipse has allowed me to see the benefits of a more restricted system. Generally speaking if I need to deal with an aerial enemy I know what to do, if I need to get an enemy far away I know what to do, regardless of what specific skills I have equipped. That certainly isn’t to say that skill choice doesn’t matter but rather that the finer details of the skills play a much larger role. Things like damage type, elemental effects, cost, cooldown, hitbox size, and more all play a role in what you want to choose and that choice will change over time. In the mid to late game, especially on hard difficulty, enemies become quite tanky if you aren’t exploiting their weaknesses, so picking skills that do so is very important. In addition, even if they aren’t hardcoded weaknesses, certain enemies require certain types of skills. For example, one enemy type teleports way whenever you get close so having an option that either approaches very quickly or hits from far away is necessary. Many late game enemy types also love blocking which are countered by specific grapple abilities. It isn’t just the enemies you have to consider however but the environment as well. The game is very adamant about attacks not being able to pierce walls so long range skills tend to have their usability severely nerfed in tight areas, allowing short range melee options to have their moment to shine. 

Just as delightful are the enemies you fight against. The game has an adaptive leveling system where the same enemy types are reused throughout the game and rank up alongside you. While often maligned in RPGs what makes it work here is the changes that come with rank. High rank enemies don’t just hit harder and die slower; but have completely new moves that in many cases feel deliberately designed to counter techniques you use in lower ranks. It makes seeing new enemy ranks both exciting and frightening as previously simple encounters become more dangerous. This also evolves alongside your own mastery of the game's movement. The enemies have simple movesets early on where any sort of combat encounter is a struggle due to the floaty movement however as you learn to move and position effectively the encounters place much more expectation in you doing so. Also high rank enemies drop better loot and getting better loot in this game feels really, really good. 

There are unfortunately some balance issues with the combat. Most notably I would say the guns in the game are way overpowered since they can stunlock just about any enemy, letting the player stay at a safe range and spam shooting until the problem goes away. Personally, I’m the kind of player who can play games in ways that are fun rather than seeking out minmaxing so I just stopped using guns. I do think that the game would improve quite a bit if the guns did not stun enemies as they do now. Having a long range, reliable, and cheap damage option is already really good, but making enemies completely unable to approach you is a bit too much. I’d also say the game suffers from a bit of a design slump in the middle. Early encounter design is very much focused on the challenge of hitting enemies at all, and your at the time limited moveset along with the floaty controls that you are still becoming accustomed to makes this a genuine challenge. As you get stronger and get a toolkit that can more effectively deal with any situation, the game transitions to encounters with genuinely challenging enemies with varied and dangerous attacks. This is a welcome change, however in my case came a little too late leaving a number of areas in the middle where I kinda just autopiloted through. The Ungerground LOOP suffers from this the most and is just a very dull area to explore. 

One thing I want to shout out is the game’s wonderful sense of humour. There’s a wonderful macabre whimsy to the way everything is delivered. The presence of death is immediately apparent in the game, with the very first enemies being zombies. It’s something that at the time feels so innocuous, as good of a first enemy as any you suppose, but the presence of the undead is apparent everywhere you go and makes the world immediately unsettling. The undead presence seeps even into the game’s items; with demonic contracts, bizarre curses, and just an actual dead body make up some of the sellable junk items you get. But don’t worry, the body’s item description makes sure to assure the reader that a memorial will be held after you sell it! The game just has great text in general honestly, and I always felt compelled to check every item description just in case there’s something funny in there, which there often is. 

All in all the game is excellent, rough for sure but absolutely worth your time. There’s definitely a lot of adjustment as you learn to play the game by its rules but once you do, you realize how much there is to love and the utter strangeness of all of it compels you to see it through. I very strongly recommend it if you have any interest in action RPGS. I sincerely hope that the dev continues to make games because this is something seriously special. 

Also you should add a way to unequip shoes so that you can see his feet again thanks.
